pos: n. (a land famous for the finest gold, reached by Solomon's navy from Eziongeber; also a son of Joktan in the table of nations)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Ophir, of uncertain meaning, first the name of a man — the eleventh son of Joktan (Gen 10:29) — and afterward of the country his descendants settled. In Scripture the word finally becomes a byword for quality: gold of Ophir is the Hebrew way of saying the best gold there is.
biblical_def: Ophir enters as a name in the table of nations, “And Ophir, and Havilah, and Jobab: all these were the sons of Joktan” (Gen 10:29), and leaves as a proverb. The trade began with Solomon and Hiram of Tyre: “And they came to Ophir, and fetched from thence gold, four hundred and twenty talents, and brought it to king Solomon” (1Ki 9:28), and the same fleet brought “great plenty of almug trees, and precious stones” (1Ki 10:11). The voyage was long — three years out and back — and it required a harbour on the Red Sea, which is why Jehoshaphat's later attempt to revive it failed before it sailed: “Jehoshaphat made ships of Tharshish to go to Ophir for gold: but they went not; for the ships were broken at Eziongeber” (1Ki 22:48). Where Ophir lay is not stated and cannot now be settled — Arabia, east Africa and India have all been argued. What Scripture cares about is the standard the name became. Job weighs wisdom against it: “It cannot be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire” (Job 28:16). The psalmist dresses the king's bride in it: “upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir” (Psa 45:9). Isaiah makes it the measure of how scarce men will be in the day of the LORD's anger: “I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir” (Isa 13:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Ophir; in sacred history it is a country famous for gold, whither the navy of Solomon sailed from Eziongeber.
webster_full: OPHIR, n. A son of Joktan, and the country peopled by his posterity.
A land renowned for gold, and for almug trees and precious stones.
Solomon's navy, with the servants of Hiram, fetched thence four hundred and twenty talents of gold.
Jehoshaphat afterward made ships to go to Ophir, but they were broken at Eziongeber.
The gold of Ophir is used in Scripture as the proverbial standard of the finest gold.
scriptures: And they came to Ophir, and fetched from thence gold, four hundred and twenty talents, and brought it to king Solomon.
Jehoshaphat made ships of Tharshish to go to Ophir for gold: but they went not; for the ships were broken at Eziongeber.
It cannot be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire.
I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this place. The principle to recover is that Scripture uses the world's highest valuation only to be outbid — wisdom, a man, and the knowledge of God are each priced above the gold of Ophir.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Ophir is a gold country whose site is unknown and nobody has contested it. What the name does in Scripture is provide a fixed point of value against which better things are measured. Job 28 is the classic passage: the chapter surveys the whole mining industry of the ancient world, men cutting shafts into the rock and turning up the earth as by fire, and then asks where wisdom shall be found — and answers that it cannot be got for gold, nor weighed against the gold of Ophir, and that “the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28:28).

The principle to recover is that the Bible does not despise wealth in order to make its point; it uses wealth as a real measure and then names something that outweighs it. Peter writes of a faith “much more precious than of gold that perisheth” (1Pe 1:7), and Christ counsels the Laodiceans to buy of Him “gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich” (Rev 3:18). A ministry that can only denounce riches has not learned this language. The Bible names the best the world can offer, grants that it is genuinely good, and then sets it in the scale against the fear of the LORD and watches the balance move.

pos: n. (a land encompassed by the river Pison in the account of Eden, where there is gold; also the name of two men in the table of nations, and a boundary of the Ishmaelite and Amalekite country)
etymology: From Hebrew Chaviylah, probably from chul, to twist or writhe, and taken by some as circle or sandy tract. The name attaches to a Cushite (Gen 10:7) and to a Joktanite (Gen 10:29), and to a region on the desert border between Egypt and Assyria.
biblical_def: Havilah is one of the four place-names in the geography of Eden, and the only one Scripture pauses to describe: “The name of the first is Pison: that is it which compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold” (Gen 2:11), and the following verse adds that the gold of that land is good, with bdellium and the onyx stone. It is a striking notice. Before the fall, before commerce, before any use for currency, Moses tells the reader that there was gold in the world and that it was good gold — created things with worth in them, waiting for men who would either steward or worship them. The name recurs as a Cushite in the sons of Ham: “And the sons of Cush; Seba, and Havilah, and Sabtah, and Raamah, and Sabtecha” (Gen 10:7), and as a Joktanite in the line of Shem (Gen 10:29), so that two peoples of the name existed. As a boundary it marks the run of the Ishmaelite settlements: “they dwelt from Havilah unto Shur, that is before Egypt, as thou goest toward Assyria” (Gen 25:18), and the same limits define Saul's Amalekite campaign: “And Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah until thou comest to Shur” (1Sa 15:7) — the very war in which he spared Agag and lost the kingdom.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Havilah; in sacred history it is a land compassed by the river Pison, where there is gold, and a boundary of the Ishmaelite country.
webster_full: HAVILAH, n. A land named in the second chapter of Genesis, compassed by the river Pison.
It is said that there is gold in that land, and that the gold is good.
Bdellium and the onyx stone are named there also.
Havilah is likewise the name of a son of Cush and of a son of Joktan.
The seed of Ishmael dwelt from Havilah unto Shur, that is before Egypt.
scriptures: Gen 2:11
The name of the first is Pison: that is it which compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold;
Gen 10:7
And the sons of Cush; Seba, and Havilah, and Sabtah, and Raamah, and Sabtecha: and the sons of Raamah; Sheba, and Dedan.
And Ophir, and Havilah, and Jobab: all these were the sons of Joktan.
And they dwelt from Havilah unto Shur, that is before Egypt, as thou goest toward Assyria: and he died in the presence of all his brethren.
corruption_summary: The land of Eden is commonly treated as mythological geography with no location in the real world. Moses writes it as a map with named rivers and a country known for its gold, and the dictionary reads it as he wrote it.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard academic handling of Genesis 2:10-14 is to call it symbolic topography — a paradise-motif dressed in place-names, not a description of anywhere. But the passage does not read like myth. It names four rivers, tells which way each runs, names the countries they compass, and pauses to record the natural products of one of them: gold, and good gold, with bdellium and onyx. That is the diction of a survey. Two of the four rivers, Hiddekel and Euphrates, are ordinary rivers of the known world and are so used everywhere else in Scripture. Moses is locating a real garden in a real world, in terrain the flood afterward wrecked beyond recovery — which is why the site cannot now be found, and is not a reason to conclude there was none.

The doctrinal weight is heavier than a map. If Eden is a symbol, Adam is a symbol, and if Adam is a symbol the whole argument of Romans 5 collapses: “For as by one man&#39;s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19). The parallel requires two historical men. Paul builds the resurrection on the same footing: “The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit” (1Co 15:45). Havilah, gold and all, is one of the small stakes driven into the ground to show that the writer thought he was describing the earth.

pos: n. (the great desert country south and east of Palestine, whose kings brought tribute to Solomon, whose merchants traded with Tyre, and in which Paul places mount Sinai)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Arab, connected with 'arabah, a desert plain or steppe, and with a root meaning to grow dark — hence the waste, the evening land. The Authorized Version also renders the people Arabians and speaks of “the mingled people that dwell in the desert”.
biblical_def: Arabia in Scripture is not a nation with a throne but a vast tract of tents, flocks and caravans, whose chiefs are called kings and whose wealth was mobile. In Solomon's day it paid: “And all the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon” (2Ch 9:14). Ezekiel lists it among the trading partners in the great lament over Tyre: “Arabia, and all the princes of Kedar, they occupied with thee in lambs, and rams, and goats: in these were they thy merchants” (Eze 27:21). Isaiah lays a burden on it and pictures the caravans driven off the roads into the scrub: “The burden upon Arabia. In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim” (Isa 21:13), and Jeremiah sets “all the kings of Arabia, and all the kings of the mingled people that dwell in the desert” (Jer 25:24) among the nations that must drink the cup. In the New Testament the name carries the whole weight of an argument. Paul, contending against the Judaizers, writes: “For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia, and answereth to Jerusalem which now is, and is in bondage with her children” (Gal 4:25). Sinai stands outside the land of promise, in the desert, and the covenant given there gendereth to bondage; the Jerusalem above is free. Paul himself went into Arabia after his conversion (Gal 1:17) and returned to Damascus, and the years there are the silence out of which the apostle to the Gentiles came.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Arabian and Arabic; in sacred history Arabia is the desert country south and east of Judea, whose kings brought gold to Solomon and in which mount Sinai stands.
webster_full: ARABIA, n. A large country of Asia, lying south and east of Judea, chiefly desert.
Its inhabitants dwelt in tents, kept flocks, and conducted the caravans of the east.
All the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon.
The princes of Kedar traded with Tyre in lambs, and rams, and goats.
The apostle Paul states that mount Sinai is in Arabia, and thither he went after his conversion.
scriptures: Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon.
The burden upon Arabia. In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim.
Arabia, and all the princes of Kedar, they occupied with thee in lambs, and rams, and goats: in these were they thy merchants.
Gal 4:25
For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia, and answereth to Jerusalem which now is, and is in bondage with her children.
corruption_summary: Galatians 4 is now widely read as an allegory that Paul invents and that carries no doctrinal weight. Paul offers it as the true sense of a real history, and the two covenants he distinguishes there are the hinge of the whole epistle.
corruption_paragraphs: It is common to hear that Paul's Hagar-and-Sarah passage is a rabbinical flourish, an ingenious allegory that a modern reader may admire and set aside. That reading takes shelter in the word allegory and ignores what Paul does with it. He does not treat Hagar and Sarah as figures rather than women; he treats two historical women, two historical sons and two actual mountains as bearing a covenantal meaning that God intended when the events happened. Sinai is in Arabia, outside the land, and the covenant made there could not give the inheritance. That is not decoration; it is the argument by which he tells the Galatians that circumcision under the law will make them debtors to the whole of it.

The doctrine at stake is the distinction between law and gospel, and the Reformed confessions guard it because everything else depends on it. The law is holy, just and good, and it cannot justify a sinner; “the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith” (Gal 3:24). Flatten Paul's Arabia into a literary device and the two covenants blur into one continuum of religious effort, which is precisely the error the epistle was written to kill. The desert where the law was given is still a desert; the Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all.

pos: n. (the country between the two rivers, from which Abraham was called, whither Abraham's servant went for a wife for Isaac, and out of which came Israel's first oppressor in the days of the judges)
etymology: Greek Mesopotamia, from mesos, middle, and potamos, river — the land between the rivers, Euphrates and Hiddekel. The Authorized Version uses it to render the Hebrew Aram-naharaim, Aram of the two rivers, and Padan-aram, the plain of Aram.
biblical_def: Mesopotamia is where the history of the covenant begins, geographically speaking. Stephen puts it in the first sentence of his defence: “The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran” (Act 7:2) — the call came in a land of settled idolatry, before Haran and long before Canaan, and it came to a man who had done nothing to deserve it. The country stays in the story as the family reservoir: “he arose, and went to Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor” (Gen 24:10), the errand that brought Rebekah home for Isaac, and thence Jacob took Leah and Rachel. Its second face is hostile. Balaam was hired out of it: Moab “hired against thee Balaam the son of Beor of Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse thee” (Deu 23:4). And the first oppression in the book of Judges came from there: “he sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia: and the children of Israel served Chushanrishathaim eight years” (Jdg 3:8), until Othniel the son of Kenaz delivered them. At Pentecost the region is named again among the languages that heard the wonderful works of God: “Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia” (Act 2:9). The land Abraham was called out of heard the gospel preached in its own tongue.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Mesopotamia as the country between the Euphrates and the Tigris; in sacred history it is the land of Abraham's calling and of Nahor's city.
webster_full: MESOPOTAMIA, n. Greek, the middle between rivers; the country lying between the Euphrates and the Tigris.
It answers to the Hebrew Aram-naharaim, that is, Syria of the two rivers.
The God of glory appeared to Abraham there, before he dwelt in Charran.
Abraham's servant went thither, unto the city of Nahor, to take a wife for Isaac.
Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia was the first oppressor of Israel in the time of the judges.
scriptures: And the servant took ten camels of the camels of his master, and departed; for all the goods of his master were in his hand: and he arose, and went to Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor.
Deu 23:4
Because they met you not with bread and with water in the way, when ye came forth out of Egypt; and because they hired against thee Balaam the son of Beor of Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse thee.
Jdg 3:8
Therefore the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia: and the children of Israel served Chushanrishathaim eight years.
Act 7:2
And he said, Men, brethren, and fathers, hearken; The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran,
corruption_summary: Abraham's call is often told as a spiritual quest — a seeker leaving idolatry behind. Scripture presents it as sovereign, unsought grace: God appeared to a man in a pagan city who was not looking for Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular telling makes Abraham a man of unusual spiritual sensitivity who grew dissatisfied with the gods of his fathers and set out to find the true One. Scripture says the opposite. Joshua tells the assembled nation plainly: “Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods” (Jos 24:2), and the next verse begins, And I took your father Abraham. Stephen's account agrees: the God of glory appeared. The initiative is entirely on God's side, exercised toward an idolater in Mesopotamia, and this is the pattern of every conversion since.

That is unconditional election as the Bible narrates rather than argues it, and Paul makes the doctrine explicit from the same family: the choice of Jacob over Esau was made before the children were born or had done any good or evil, “that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth” (Rom 9:11). The seeker-narrative is attractive because it leaves the sinner something to have contributed. The land between the rivers refutes it: God spoke first, to a man who served other gods, and the whole covenant follows from that appearing.

pos: n. (the second son of Shem, and the Assyrian people and land called by his name in the poetical and prophetical books)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Ashshur, the eponymous father of the Assyrians, whose name was also borne by their chief god and their first capital. The Authorized Version keeps Asshur where the Hebrew is poetical or archaic and uses Assyria or the Assyrian in ordinary narrative — the same people under two English dresses.
biblical_def: Asshur is first a man, listed among the sons of Shem: “The children of Shem; Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram” (Gen 10:22), and named in the account of Nimrod's expansion: “Out of that land went forth Asshur, and builded Nineveh, and the city Rehoboth, and Calah” (Gen 10:11). Thereafter the name is the nation. Balaam saw it from the hills of Moab before Assyria was anything, and prophesied its rise and its fall in a single oracle: the Kenite shall be wasted “until Asshur shall carry thee away captive” (Num 24:22), and then “ships shall come from the coast of Chittim, and shall afflict Asshur, and shall afflict Eber, and he also shall perish for ever” (Num 24:24). Asaph lists it in the confederacy against Israel: “Assur also is joined with them: they have holpen the children of Lot” (Psa 83:8). Ezekiel puts it in the merchant-roll of Tyre (Eze 27:23) and figures it as a cedar of Lebanon overtopping every tree of the field, cut down for its pride (Eze 31:3-14). And Hosea uses the name in the great sentence of the returning remnant, where repentance is spelled out as the renunciation of three false helps at once: “Asshur shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses: neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, Ye are our gods: for in thee the fatherless findeth mercy” (Hos 14:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Asshur; in sacred history he is the son of Shem from whom Assyria took its name, and the name stands for that nation in the poets and prophets.
webster_full: ASSHUR, n. The second son of Shem, and the founder of the Assyrian nation.
Out of the land of Shinar he went forth and builded Nineveh, Rehoboth and Calah.
The name is used in the Scriptures for the Assyrian people and empire.
Balaam foretold that Asshur should carry the Kenite away captive, and should himself perish.
Hosea puts into the mouth of the penitent, Asshur shall not save us.
scriptures: Out of that land went forth Asshur, and builded Nineveh, and the city Rehoboth, and Calah,
The children of Shem; Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram.
And ships shall come from the coast of Chittim, and shall afflict Asshur, and shall afflict Eber, and he also shall perish for ever.
Hos 14:3
Asshur shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses: neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, Ye are our gods: for in thee the fatherless findeth mercy.
corruption_summary: The prophetic oracles against Asshur are commonly dated after the events they announce, on the rule that genuine prediction does not occur. Scripture presents them as prophecy given beforehand, and rests the credibility of the LORD Himself on exactly that claim.
corruption_paragraphs: Balaam's oracle naming Asshur, and Chittim afterward afflicting Asshur, is routinely assigned a date late enough to make it a description of what had already happened — and the same operation is performed on Isaiah's Assyrian chapters, on Daniel, and wherever else a prophecy proves specific. The rule being applied is not a finding of evidence but a philosophical premise: that God does not tell His prophets what He will do. Once the premise is granted, every predictive text must be redated, and the redating is then presented as the result of scholarship rather than its starting assumption.

The LORD Himself makes prediction the test of deity, and does so in the sharpest terms: “Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10), and He challenges the idols to do it: “Shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods” (Isa 41:23). Deuteronomy 18 makes fulfilment the criterion by which Israel was to know a true prophet. A hermeneutic that must date every fulfilled prophecy after the fact has not read the book carefully; it has decided in advance what the book is allowed to be.

pos: n. (a place named twice in Scripture as a source of the finest gold, once for the overlaying of idols and once for the girdle of the man clothed in linen)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Uphaz, of unknown site and uncertain derivation; some have supposed it a variant of Ophir, and others a term of quality rather than a place. Whatever its geography, its use in Scripture is fixed: gold of Uphaz means refined gold of the highest sort.
biblical_def: Uphaz occurs exactly twice, and the two passages set the same substance in two opposite frames. Jeremiah, mocking the customs of the heathen, describes the manufacture of an idol from raw material to finished article: “Silver spread into plates is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz, the work of the workman, and of the hands of the founder: blue and purple is their clothing: they are all the work of cunning men” (Jer 10:9). The finest metal on earth, worked by the best craftsmen alive, dressed in the costliest dye — and the prophet's verdict a few lines later is that they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Daniel uses the same gold of a very different figure. Standing by the river Hiddekel he sees a man clothed in linen “whose loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz” (Dan 10:5), with a body like the beryl, a face as the appearance of lightning, and eyes as lamps of fire, at whose voice the prophet fell into a deep sleep with his face toward the ground. The gold that could not make a god is fit to gird one who comes from God. Uphaz is therefore a small word with a large use: it marks the highest earthly value, and Scripture spends it once on a fraud and once on a glory.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Uphaz; in sacred history it is a place from which the finest gold was brought, named by Jeremiah and by Daniel.
webster_full: UPHAZ, n. A country or region named in the Scriptures as a source of gold.
Its situation is unknown; some have supposed it the same with Ophir.
Jeremiah names gold from Uphaz among the materials of the idols of the heathen.
Daniel saw a man clothed in linen whose loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz.
The phrase denotes gold of the purest and most excellent kind.
scriptures: Jer 10:9

Silver spread into plates is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz, the work of the workman, and of the hands of the founder: blue and purple is their clothing: they are all the work of cunning men.
Dan 10:5
Then I lifted up mine eyes, and looked, and behold a certain man clothed in linen, whose loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz:
Jer 10:5
They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good.
Dan 10:6

His body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire, and his arms and his feet like in colour to polished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this place. The principle to recover is that the value of a material is never the measure of the thing made from it, and that the best of the earth spent on a lie is still a lie.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Uphaz is an unlocated gold country and nobody has contested it. What Jeremiah 10 sets against the reader is the futility of expense. The chapter is deliberately detailed about cost and craftsmanship: imported silver, gold from Uphaz, a founder, a workman, cunning men, blue and purple clothing, nails and hammers to keep the thing from toppling. Every step is expensive and skilled, and the summary is contemptuous: “they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good” (Jer 10:5).

The principle to recover is that quality of workmanship does not sanctify an object of worship, and that this applies to more than statues. Money, artistry, technical excellence and cultural prestige can all be poured into a form of religion that has no God in it, and the result is the more convincing for the expense. Set beside it Daniel's vision, where the same gold girds a living person of terrible glory: “His body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire” (Dan 10:6). The difference between the two passages is not the metal. It is whether anyone is there.

“Girded with fine gold of Uphaz” — the same gold on one who could speak.

pos: n. (the place whose gold garnished the house Solomon built, named once only in Scripture)
etymology: From Hebrew Parvayim, of unknown site; the dual ending has suggested to some an Arabian district of two parts, and to others a general term for gold of a particular refinement. It occurs one time in the whole Bible, at the building of the temple.
biblical_def: Parvaim is a single word in a single verse, and everything about it belongs to the house of the LORD. The Chronicler is describing the finishing of the most holy place, and interrupts a list of measurements to name the source of the metal: “And he garnished the house with precious stones for beauty: and the gold was gold of Parvaim” (2Ch 3:6). Kings records the same work from the other side, without the place-name but with the totality: “And the whole house he overlaid with gold, until he had finished all the house: also the whole altar that was by the oracle he overlaid with gold” (1Ki 6:22). The temple was not gilded in patches. Floor, walls, doors, the partition of chains before the oracle, the altar — all overlaid, and studded with precious stones, and where the finest of that gold came from, the Chronicler tells us. He does not tell us where Parvaim was, and the site has never been recovered. That is worth noticing about a book often accused of embroidering: a writer inventing splendour has no reason to invent an obscure and unexplained proper noun. He records it because it was in the record, the way a builder's account names a quarry.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Parvaim; in sacred history it is the place whence came the gold with which Solomon garnished the house of the LORD.
webster_full: PARVAIM, n. A place named once in the Scriptures, in the second book of Chronicles.
The gold with which Solomon garnished the house was gold of Parvaim.
The situation of the place is wholly unknown to us.
Some have supposed it a district of Arabia, and others a term of quality in gold.
The whole house, floor, walls and doors, was overlaid with gold, and set with precious stones for beauty.
scriptures: And he garnished the house with precious stones for beauty: and the gold was gold of Parvaim.
So Solomon overlaid the house within with pure gold: and he made a partition by the chains of gold before the oracle; and he overlaid it with gold.
And the whole house he overlaid with gold, until he had finished all the house: also the whole altar that was by the oracle he overlaid with gold.

And he made the most holy house, the length whereof was according to the breadth of the house, twenty cubits, and the breadth thereof twenty cubits: and he overlaid it with fine gold, amounting to six hundred talents.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this place. The principle to recover is that God commanded costly beauty in His own worship, and that the regulative principle governs the manner of worship without requiring meanness in it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Parvaim is a gold source named once and nobody has contested it. What the verse sets against a certain strain of piety is the fact that God Himself specified expense. The gold of the most holy place was not the extravagance of a king indulging himself; the pattern came from the LORD by the hand of David, and the Chronicler weighs the gold to six hundred talents (2Ch 3:8). Beauty in the worship of God is commanded, not merely tolerated, and the tabernacle before it was the same — blue, purple, scarlet, fine twined linen, cunning work, and men filled with the Spirit of God to do it.

The principle to recover holds two things together that are often set at odds. Worship is governed by the regulative principle: what God has commanded is required, what He has not commanded is not permitted, and no man may add a ceremony because he finds it moving. But within what He commands, He has never asked for shabbiness. The same Scripture that forbids will-worship records six hundred talents of the gold of Parvaim on the walls of the oracle. A congregation may meet in a plain room and worship rightly; what it may not do is conclude that carelessness is humility, or that God is honoured by giving Him the leavings.

pos: n. (a distant land named by Isaiah, from which the LORD promises His people shall come — the farthest point of the compass in the prophet's roll-call of the returning)
etymology: From Hebrew Siyniym, a plural gentilic of unknown reference. It has been identified with the far east and with a southern district of Egypt; no identification is certain, and the uncertainty is itself part of the effect, since the word functions in the verse as the place beyond the places you can name.
biblical_def: Sinim occurs once. Isaiah is in the middle of the Servant songs, and the LORD has just told His Servant that raising up the tribes of Jacob is too small a commission: “I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth” (Isa 49:6). The promise of ingathering that follows sweeps the horizon: “Behold, these shall come from far: and, lo, these from the north and from the west; and these from the land of Sinim” (Isa 49:12). North, west, and then a name at the edge of the known world. Whether Isaiah meant the Chinese, as many older expositors held, or a remote southern people, the function of the word in the sentence is not in doubt: it is the farthest place, put in to say that no distance is outside the reach of the covenant. The context forbids reading it as a promise about Jewish exiles only. The Servant is given for a covenant of the people and a light to the Gentiles, and Paul and Barnabas quote this very verse at Antioch in Pisidia when they turn to the nations (Act 13:47). Sinim is the Old Testament's way of writing what John saw: a great multitude which no man could number, of all nations and kindreds and people and tongues.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Sinim; in sacred history it is a far country named by Isaiah among the places from which the people of God shall come.
webster_full: SINIM, n. A distant land named in the forty-ninth chapter of Isaiah.
The prophet says, these from the north and from the west; and these from the land of Sinim.
The place has not been certainly identified by expositors.
Many of the older writers understood it of the Chinese, at the eastern limit of the world then known.
It stands in the verse for the remotest region, whence the LORD will yet gather his people.
scriptures: Isa 49:6

And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.
Isa 49:8

Thus saith the LORD, In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in a day of salvation have I helped thee: and I will preserve thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, to establish the earth, to cause to inherit the desolate heritages;
Behold, these shall come from far: and, lo, these from the north and from the west; and these from the land of Sinim.
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
corruption_summary: Isaiah's Servant songs are commonly divided among a second and third author writing after the exile, and read as consolation for returning Jews rather than as prophecy of a world-wide salvation. The dictionary holds one Isaiah, and reads the Servant as Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical convention assigns Isaiah 40-55 to an anonymous exilic writer and 56-66 to a third hand, chiefly because the chapters address a captivity that lay a century and a half beyond the prophet's lifetime. The reasoning is the same premise applied to Asshur and to Daniel — that specific prediction cannot occur, therefore any text that contains it must postdate its subject. Scripture itself knows nothing of a second or third Isaiah. The New Testament quotes freely from both halves of the book and attributes both to the one prophet: John cites chapter 53 and chapter 6 in adjacent verses and says of both, “Esaias said again” (Joh 12:39). One prophet, one book.

The reduction of the Servant to the nation of Israel, or to the prophet himself, empties the passage in a second way. The Servant is given “for a covenant of the people” (Isa 49:8) — a person who is himself a covenant — and he is a light to the Gentiles that God's salvation may reach the end of the earth. Israel could not be given as a covenant to Israel. The apostles read the verse as fulfilled in Christ and in the mission that followed Him, and Sinim, wherever it lay, is Isaiah's promise that the gospel would not stop at any border a map could draw.

pos: n. (the waste or desert, used in the Authorized Version as the name of the wilderness tract south-east of Hebron where David hid from Saul, and of the desolation seen from Pisgah)
etymology: From Hebrew Yeshiymon, from yasham, to be desolate or laid waste — hence the waste, the desolation. The Authorized Version treats it as a proper name in the four places where it stands with the article; elsewhere the same word is rendered simply the desert or the wilderness.
biblical_def: Jeshimon is the parched country falling away toward the Dead Sea, and it is the landscape of David's outlaw years. The Ziphites betrayed him twice by describing exactly where he was in it: “Doth not David hide himself with us in strong holds in the wood, in the hill of Hachilah, which is on the south of Jeshimon?” (1Sa 23:19), and again later, “Doth not David hide himself in the hill of Hachilah, which is before Jeshimon?” (1Sa 26:1). Saul brought three thousand chosen men into that waste after one man, and pitched in the same hill: “And Saul pitched in the hill of Hachilah, which is before Jeshimon, by the way. But David abode in the wilderness” (1Sa 26:3) — and it was there, in the night, that David stood over the sleeping king with Abishai urging one stroke, and would not put forth his hand against the LORD's anointed. The name occurs also in the itinerary of Moses, describing the view eastward from the heights of Moab: “to the top of Pisgah, which looketh toward Jeshimon” (Num 21:20). Both settings are the same kind of ground: emptiness, heat, no water, no cover but rock — and in both, the LORD is dealing with a man about a kingdom.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Jeshimon; in sacred history it is the waste or desert country south-east of Judah, where David hid from Saul, and the desolation seen from Pisgah.
webster_full: JESHIMON, n. The waste, the desolation; a name of the desert tract toward the Dead Sea.
David hid himself in the strong holds in the hill of Hachilah, which is before Jeshimon.
The Ziphites twice discovered him to Saul in that wilderness.
There Saul pitched with three thousand chosen men of Israel.
The top of Pisgah in the country of Moab is said to look toward Jeshimon.
scriptures: Then came up the Ziphites to Saul to Gibeah, saying, Doth not David hide himself with us in strong holds in the wood, in the hill of Hachilah, which is on the south of Jeshimon?
And they arose, and went to Ziph before Saul: but David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the plain on the south of Jeshimon.
And Saul pitched in the hill of Hachilah, which is before Jeshimon, by the way. But David abode in the wilderness, and he saw that Saul came after him into the wilderness.
And from Bamoth in the valley, that is in the country of Moab, to the top of Pisgah, which looketh toward Jeshimon.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this place. The principle to recover is that the wilderness is a school God builds His servants in, and that the years of hiding are not an interruption of the calling but part of it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Jeshimon is a desert tract and nobody has contested it. What it sets against the modern expectation is the shape of a calling. David was anointed king as a boy and then spent years in caves and strongholds in a waste that could not feed him, hunted by the man he refused to kill, writing psalms in it — the fifty-fourth is headed by the Ziphites' betrayal. He did not receive the throne and then face hardship; he faced the hardship as the road to the throne, and Scripture treats the interval as formation rather than delay.

The principle to recover is that God tests and trains in the waste as a matter of settled practice. Israel was led forty years in the wilderness “to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart” (Deu 8:2); Moses kept sheep in Midian for forty; the Lord Himself was led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted. A ministry philosophy that reads every barren season as a sign of God's displeasure, or as a problem to be escaped, has no category for Jeshimon — and it will produce men who have never learned in the dark what David learned there, that he could spare Saul's life because the kingdom was not his to seize.

pos: n. (the firstborn of Ishmael and the Arabian tribe descended from him, whose rams Isaiah sees brought up with acceptance on the altar of the LORD; written also Nebajoth)
etymology: From Hebrew Nebayoth, of uncertain sense, connected by some with nabat, to look or behold, and hence heights. The Authorized Version spells the man Nebajoth in Genesis and Chronicles and the tribe Nebaioth in Isaiah; it is one name.
biblical_def: Nebaioth is the eldest of the twelve princes of Ishmael: “the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebajoth; and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam” (Gen 25:13), repeated in the Chronicler's roll (1Ch 1:29). Esau married into the family, taking “Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael Abraham's son, the sister of Nebajoth, to be his wife” (Gen 28:9) — a marriage made to please his father after he saw that the daughters of Canaan pleased him not, and one of the plainest pictures in Genesis of religion attempted as strategy. The tribe became a people of flocks and tents in the northern Arabian desert, brother-tribe to Kedar, and there Isaiah finds them. In the great chapter of the Gentiles streaming to Zion, the desert clans come not as tribute-payers but as worshippers: “All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered together unto thee, the rams of Nebaioth shall minister unto thee: they shall come up with acceptance on mine altar, and I will glorify the house of my glory” (Isa 60:7). The sons of Hagar's son bring their beasts to the altar of the God of Abraham, and the sacrifice is accepted. It is a startling promise: the line that went out from the covenant household comes back into the courts of the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Nebaioth; in sacred history he is the firstborn of Ishmael, and an Arabian tribe of his name whose rams Isaiah sees offered on the altar of God.
webster_full: NEBAIOTH, n. The firstborn son of Ishmael, written also Nebajoth.
He was one of the twelve princes of the Ishmaelites, by their towns and their castles.
His sister Mahalath was taken to wife by Esau, the son of Isaac.
The tribe of his name dwelt in the Arabian desert, and were keepers of flocks.
Isaiah foretells that the rams of Nebaioth shall come up with acceptance on the altar of the LORD.
scriptures: And these are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, according to their generations: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebajoth; and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam,
Gen 28:9
Then went Esau unto Ishmael, and took unto the wives which he had Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael Abraham's son, the sister of Nebajoth, to be his wife.
These are their generations: The firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth; then Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam,
Isa 60:7

All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered together unto thee, the rams of Nebaioth shall minister unto thee: they shall come up with acceptance on mine altar, and I will glorify the house of my glory.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 60 is often read as a promise of national restoration for ethnic Israel with the nations reduced to tributaries. The chapter is a prophecy of the church gathered out of every people, the Gentiles coming not as vassals but as worshippers whose offerings are accepted.
corruption_paragraphs: The dispensational reading of Isaiah 60 makes the chapter a description of a future millennial Jerusalem receiving the wealth of subject nations, with the sacrificial language taken as a literal restored temple service. That framework was unknown to the church until the nineteenth century and appears in no Reformation confession. Read the verse as it stands: the rams of Nebaioth minister, and they come up with acceptance on God's altar. These are not tribute animals herded in by a defeated people; they are the offerings of worshippers received by the LORD, from the very stock that went out of Abraham's house with Hagar.

The apostles read such promises as fulfilled in the gathering of the Gentiles into Christ. Paul speaks of his own ministry as a priestly service, “ministering the gospel of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost” (Rom 15:16) — which is Isaiah 60:7 in New Testament dress. Peter tells scattered believers they are “an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ” (1Pe 2:5). One altar remains and one sacrifice has been offered upon it; what the flocks of Kedar and the rams of Nebaioth prefigure is desert tribes brought near by the blood of Christ and worshipping with the household they were once outside of.
